entries.title: ANALYSIS HEURISTIC
entries.body:
A chain analysis heuristic on Bitcoin is a family of empirical methods used to trace the flows of bitcoins on the blockchain based on characteristics observed in transactions. A heuristic is a practical approach to solving problems, often through approximate methods, but which represents a solution that is good enough to reach a given goal. These heuristics make it possible to obtain fairly reliable results, but never with absolute precision. In other words, chain analysis always involves a dimension of likelihood in the conclusions drawn. For example, one can estimate with more or less certainty that two addresses belong to the same entity, but total certainty will always be out of reach. The whole objective of chain analysis lies precisely in the aggregation of various heuristics in order to minimize the risk of error. It is in a way an accumulation of evidence that allows us to get closer to reality. In this framework, a distinction is made between internal heuristics and external heuristics.

Internal heuristics focus on characteristics specific to the inside of an individual transaction. Their analysis includes elements such as UTXO amounts, the scripts used, versions, or *locktimes*. For example, the round payment heuristic makes it possible to identify a transaction output as likely being a payment if its amount is a round number. These heuristics often make it possible to identify the change (the money that returns to the same user) and thus to continue tracing.

External heuristics, for their part, analyze similarities and characteristics beyond the transaction itself. They encompass the entire environment of the transaction. For example, address reuse across several transactions is an external heuristic. The CIOH is another one.

entries.title: BLOCK HEIGHT
entries.body: Refers to the sequence number of a particular block relative to the first block, known as the "Genesis block", which is indexed at height zero. This indicator gives us the number of blocks that precede the block under study. For example, if a block is at height 650,000, it means that there are 650,000 blocks preceding it. Block height is used to identify a specific block within the blockchain. Contrary to a widespread belief, block height does not determine which chain is valid, because nodes synchronize on the chain that has accumulated the most work, and not on the longest chain.

entries.title: HALVING
HARD FORK
entries.body:
A modification of the protocol rules in a non-backward-compatible way. This modification results in a permanent split of the Bitcoin node network into two distinct groups: the nodes with the update and the nodes without the update. This split materializes as the division of the original blockchain into two distinct blockchains, which nonetheless share a common history, hence the use of the term "fork", which can be translated into French as "embranchement, bifurcation".

A modification is said to be non-backward-compatible when it is either extensive, meaning that it removes or makes less restrictive certain protocol rules, or bilateral, meaning that it adds rules that are incompatible with the old ones. In other words, a hard fork is observed when some nodes make an invalid block become valid. The result is the formation of a new version of the protocol, which can either replace the original Bitcoin if a majority is found, or become an independent altcoin if it is only used on the fringes. For example, Bitcoin Cash (BCH) is a hard fork of Bitcoin. The fork took place at block no. 478,559, on August 1, 2017.

entries.title: HARDWARE WALLET
entries.body:
A hardware wallet is an electronic device dedicated to securing and managing the private keys of a Bitcoin wallet. These devices are designed to provide enhanced security compared to software wallets, which run on general-purpose machines directly connected to the internet. Hardware wallets store the mnemonic phrase offline, on hardware with a tiny attack surface, which isolates it from potentially vulnerable environments. When a transaction is made, the hardware wallet signs the transaction inside the device itself, without exposing the private key to the outside. Once the transaction is signed, it is transmitted to the Bitcoin network to be confirmed and included in the Bitcoin blockchain. Among the most popular hardware wallet models are: Ledger, Trezor, Coldcard, Passport, BitBox, Satochip, Jade or SeedSigner (non-exhaustive list).

*Some bitcoiners prefer the term "signing device" ("périphérique de signature" in French), in order to avoid giving the impression that the bitcoins are physically located inside the wallet.*

entries.title: HASH160
entries.body:
A cryptographic function used on Bitcoin notably to generate Legacy and SegWit v0 receiving addresses. It combines two hash functions that are executed successively on the input: first SHA256, then RIPEMD160. The output of this function is therefore 160 bits.
```math
HASH160(x)\ =\ RIPEMD160(SHA256(x))
```

entries.title: HASH256
entries.body:
A cryptographic function used for various applications on Bitcoin. It consists of applying the SHA256 function twice to the input data. The message is passed through SHA256 a first time, and the result of this operation is used as the input to pass through SHA256 a second time. The output of this function is therefore 256 bits.
```math
HASH256(x)\ =\ SHA256(SHA256(x))
```

entries.title: HASHBOARD
entries.body: The electronic board that is the main component of an ASIC miner. Each hashboard contains the hashing chips (the ASICs properly speaking) that perform the `SHA256` calculations necessary for mining Bitcoin. A typical ASIC miner, such as an Antminer S9 or S19, generally incorporates three hashboards connected to a control board.

entries.title: HASHCASH
HASHER
entries.body: In the context of mining pools, participants are often referred to as "hashers". The main task of these individual miners is to hash block *templates* provided by the pool's server, searching for hashes that satisfy the difficulty target defined for *shares*, and not Bitcoin's. The rest of the mining process, which includes the actual construction of blocks, the selection of transactions, and the verification and broadcast of the valid proof of work according to Bitcoin's own difficulty, is carried out directly by the pools.

entries.title: HASHRATE
entries.body:
An indicator of the network's computing power, measured in hashes per second (H/s). It indicates the ability of miners to perform hashing operations as part of proof of work. A high hashrate means greater security of Bitcoin's economic history and greater resistance to attacks, since a large amount of computing power would be required to compromise the network. 

The hashrate is also indicative of the competition among miners: the higher the hashrate, the greater the mining difficulty, which influences the distribution of rewards, and therefore the profitability of miners. It is thus a key indicator of the health and security of the Bitcoin system. In the same way that the hashrate is used to measure the overall computing power of the Bitcoin network, it can also be used to measure the computing power of a machine, a mining farm or a mining pool.

entries.title: HASHRATE HIJACKING
entries.body:
An attack that consists of diverting a miner's computing power to a destination controlled by the attacker, without the miner being aware of it. This attack is possible when the communication between the miner and the mining pool's server is not encrypted. An attacker positioned between the two (man-in-the-middle attack) can intercept the exchanged data and replace the legitimate pool's address with their own, thereby redirecting the miner's hashrate to their benefit.

Hashrate hijacking is facilitated by the fact that the Stratum V1 protocol transmits data in clear text, without authentication or encryption. This vulnerability motivated the development of Stratum V2, which incorporates AEAD encryption to secure communications between miners and pools, making this type of attack much more difficult.

entries.title: HD - HIERARCHICAL-DETERMINISTIC
entries.body: Said of a Bitcoin wallet that uses a single piece of information (the seed) to generate a multitude of public and private key pairs in a sequential and reproducible manner. This way of managing keys is defined by the BIP-0032 standard. The main advantage of HD wallets is that they allow users to have a multitude of different key pairs, notably in order to avoid address reuse, while being able to regenerate all of them from a single piece of information. This structure is called hierarchical because it makes it possible to create a tree-like organization of multiple keys and addresses from a single seed. And it is deterministic in the sense that each seed always generates the same sequence of keys in any wallet compliant with this system.

entries.title: HEADERS-FIRST SYNC
entries.body: An initial synchronization method (IBD) introduced in Bitcoin Core 0.10.0, which consists of first downloading the headers of all blocks before downloading the full blocks themselves. This method replaced *blocks-first* synchronization, used by earlier versions of Bitcoin Core, which downloaded blocks sequentially from a single peer.

entries.title: HEXADECIMAL
entries.body: A base-16 numeral system, which therefore uses 16 distinct symbols to represent numbers. The first 10 symbols are the digits 0 to 9, identical to those of the decimal system (base 10), and the next six symbols are represented by the letters A to F. Thus, A represents the number 10, B represents 11, up to F which represents 15. This system is particularly used in computing, because it offers a more concise representation of binary numbers (base 2), and each hexadecimal digit represents exactly 4 bits, which simplifies conversions. This numeral system is very often found to represent information on Bitcoin.

entries.title: HMAC-SHA512
entries.body:
`HMAC-SHA512` is the acronym for "*Hash-based Message Authentication Code - Secure Hash Algorithm 512*". It is a cryptographic algorithm used to verify the integrity and authenticity of messages exchanged between two parties. It combines the cryptographic hash function `SHA512` with a shared secret key to generate a unique message authentication code (MAC) for each message.

In the context of Bitcoin, the natural use of `HMAC-SHA512` is slightly diverted. This algorithm is used in the deterministic and hierarchical derivation process of a wallet's tree of cryptographic keys. `HMAC-SHA512` is notably used to go from the seed to the master key, then for each derivation from a parent pair to child pairs. This algorithm is also found within another derivation algorithm, named `PBKDF2`, used to go from the recovery phrase and the passphrase to the seed.

entries.title: HODL
entries.body: A popular term in the Bitcoin community that refers to keeping one's bitcoins for the long term, despite market volatility, and not selling them. The term originated from a typo in [a message posted in 2013 on the BitcoinTalk forum](https://bitcointalk.org/index.php?topic=375643.msg4022997#msg4022997) by the user *GameKyuubi*, who seemed to be intoxicated, in which they wrote "I AM HODLING" instead of "I AM HOLDING", which means "to keep" in English. This word quickly became a meme and a slogan.

entries.title: HODL HODL
entries.body: A peer-to-peer (P2P) bitcoin exchange platform that allows users to buy and sell bitcoins directly between themselves, without a custodial intermediary. Founded in 2016, Hodl Hodl distinguishes itself from centralized exchange platforms by the fact that it never holds users' funds. Transactions are secured through a 2-of-3 multisig *escrow* system: the bitcoins are locked in a multisignature address associated with three keys (buyer, seller and Hodl Hodl), of which two are enough to release the funds. This mechanism reduces counterparty risk while allowing exchanges without a mandatory KYC procedure. Hodl Hodl also organizes the "Baltic Honeybadger Conference", an annual event dedicated to Bitcoin.

entries.title: HODL INVOICE
entries.body:
A particular type of Lightning invoice in which the recipient receives the payment but does not immediately reveal the *preimage* to the network. The payment thus remains "suspended": the funds are locked in the HTLCs along the route, without the recipient definitively collecting them. The recipient can then choose to settle the invoice by releasing the *preimage*, or to cancel it in order to automatically refund the sender.

*Hodl invoices* are useful for refundable deposits, online auctions, escrow systems or any mechanism requiring conditional confirmation before final settlement. They exploit the very nature of HTLCs: as long as the secret is not revealed, the payment can be canceled at no cost.

entries.title: HOME MINING
entries.body: The practice of operating, as an individual, one or more ASICs in a residential environment rather than in an industrial data center. Some manufacturers offer devices specifically designed for home use, with reduced noise levels and compact form factors. Heat reuse solutions are also developing: ASICs integrated into radiators or water heaters make it possible to reuse the heat produced by mining for home heating, which offsets the energy cost.

entries.title: HONG KONG ROUNDTABLE
entries.body:
A historic event of the Blocksize War that took place on February 20, 2016, in Hong Kong. It was an important meeting between Bitcoin Core developers and miners to discuss the scalability of the system and the strategy to adopt in order to scale it. Tensions were high before the meeting, notably because of the rise of Bitcoin Classic, a *hard fork* proposal backed by Gavin Andresen that aimed to increase the block size to 2 MB. At this meeting, influential figures in the ecosystem took part in the discussions, including Jihan Wu and Micree Zhan, the co-founders of Bitmain, Adam Back, the president of Blockstream, as well as Luke Dashjr, Matt Corallo and Peter Todd.

The miners, frustrated by the lack of progress, threatened to support Bitcoin Classic if a 2 MB *hard fork* was not implemented. The developers defended SegWit as a viable solution. After hours of tense negotiations, an agreement was reached, stipulating that the Bitcoin Core developers would work on a *hard fork* after the implementation of SegWit. This agreement was supposed to ease tensions, but it ultimately created more mistrust and confusion. Each side interpreted the agreement differently, which exacerbated the divisions within the community. Although this agreement temporarily slowed the momentum of Bitcoin Classic, it was seen by many as an unsatisfying and clumsy solution.

entries.title: HOSTED CHANNEL
entries.body:
A Lightning channel that is not anchored in an on-chain transaction, unlike classic channels. A *hosted channel*, also called a “custodial channel” or “virtual channel”, does not rely on any funding transaction on the Bitcoin blockchain: it exists only at the Lightning protocol level, with no on-chain settlement guarantee.

Its operation involves two asymmetric roles: a host, which provides the channel with liquidity on its side, and a client, which uses this channel to access the Lightning network. The funds remain in the host's custody, which makes the model custodial. However, compared to traditional custodial wallets, *hosted channels* offer additional guarantees: the client generates its own invoices and controls the payment preimages, which makes fraud detectable. The host and the client exchange mutually signed state data, which provides cryptographic proof of the balance owed. Opening and closing these channels costs nothing in mining fees, which makes it easier to onboard new users onto the Lightning Network at a lower cost.

entries.title: HRP - HUMAN READABLE PART
entries.body:
The HRP, for “*Human Readable Part*”, is a component of bech32 and bech32m receiving addresses (SegWit v0 and SegWit v1). The HRP refers to the portion of the address that is specifically formatted to be easily read and interpreted by humans. Let's take the example of a bech32 Bitcoin address:

```text
bc1qar0srrr7xfkvy5l643lydnw9re59gtzzwf5mdq
```

In this address, the initial `bc` represents the HRP. This prefix makes it possible to identify at a glance that this string of characters presented to us is a Bitcoin address and nothing else.

entries.title: HSM
entries.body:
Acronym for “Hardware Security Module”. It is a physical device dedicated to the secure management of cryptographic keys. An HSM performs key generation, signing and encryption operations in a tamper-resistant hardware environment, designed to withstand attempts at physical or logical extraction of the secrets it contains.

In the context of Bitcoin, HSMs are mainly used by companies and exchange platforms that manage large volumes of funds. They make it possible to sign Bitcoin transactions securely without the private keys ever leaving the protected perimeter of the module. Unlike *hardware wallets* intended for individuals, HSMs are industrial-grade equipment, often compliant with security certifications such as FIPS 140-2, and they are designed to operate in server environments or data centers.

An HSM is therefore distinguished from a *hardware wallet* by its use: it is designed for server environments and high-frequency automated operations, whereas a *hardware wallet* is intended for individual, interactive use. This difference in use also implies a difference in deployment: the HSM is integrated into a network infrastructure, whereas the *hardware wallet* is a personal device connected occasionally.

entries.title: HTLC
HTLC ENDORSEMENT
entries.body:
A local reputation mechanism on the Lightning Network designed to mitigate channel jamming attacks (*channel jamming*). Its principle consists of letting each routing node mark an incoming HTLC as “endorsed” or not, depending on the profitability history of the peer forwarding it.

When a node receives an HTLC from a peer that has proven reliable and profitable in the past, it can pass this endorsement on to the next hop. Endorsed HTLCs then benefit from priority access to two limited resources of each channel: HTLC *slots* (the maximum number of pending payments) and available liquidity. A share of these resources is reserved exclusively for endorsed HTLCs, while the rest remains accessible to all.

This mechanism creates an economic deterrent against attackers. A peer that carries out a *jamming* attack reduces its perceived profitability to its neighbors, which prevents its future HTLCs from obtaining endorsement and therefore access to the protected resources. Honest nodes, whose payments resolve normally, on the other hand keep their endorsement status. The approach is purely local: each node independently evaluates its peers, with no global reputation registry.

entries.title: HUMAN RIGHTS FOUNDATION
entries.body: A nonpartisan nonprofit organization founded in 2005 by Thor Halvorssen, dedicated to promoting human rights around the world, with a particular focus on authoritarian societies. Since 2020, the foundation has managed a *Bitcoin Development Fund* that finances open source projects aimed at improving Bitcoin's privacy, decentralization and accessibility. The HRF considers Bitcoin a tool of financial emancipation for populations living under authoritarian regimes, where access to the traditional banking system is restricted or monitored. The foundation also organizes educational events around Bitcoin and individual freedoms.

entries.title: HWI
entries.body: Acronym for “*Hardware Wallet Interface*”. It is a standardized interface allowing integration and interaction between Bitcoin wallet management software and hardware wallets. More precisely, HWI is both a Python library and a command-line tool. It facilitates communication between these components by using PSBTs (partially signed Bitcoin transactions) and possibly Descriptors (output script descriptors). This interface was first developed for Bitcoin Core, then it became a standard used by most wallet software.

entries.title: HYDRO COOLING
entries.body: A cooling system for ASICs that uses a closed loop in which water circulates through cooling blocks, pipes, then a radiator. The goal is to extract heat from the components and maintain a good temperature for their operation.

entries.title: HYPERBITCOINIZATION
entries.body:
A theoretical concept describing a process of massive and irreversible adoption of Bitcoin as the dominant currency worldwide, gradually replacing fiat currencies. The term was popularized by Daniel Krawisz in 2014, who described it as a voluntary transition from an inferior currency to a superior one, or more precisely as a “Bitcoin-induced currency demonetization” (*Bitcoin-induced currency demonetization*).

Hyperbitcoinization assumes a scenario in which the loss of trust in fiat currencies (due to inflation, financial control or monetary instability) pushes individuals and institutions to adopt Bitcoin massively. Hyperbitcoinization would be a voluntary and decentralized movement, in which each individual freely chooses to migrate to a sounder monetary standard.

This concept is debated within the Bitcoin community itself: some consider it an inevitable long-term goal, while others see it as a theoretical ideal that is unlikely in its absolute form, Bitcoin being able to coexist with other monetary systems, or else simply remaining a currency used at the margins, solely in the counter-economy.

entries.title: HYPERINFLATION
entries.body:
An economic phenomenon characterized by an extremely rapid and uncontrollable rise in prices. Hyperinflation occurs when a government or a central bank issues money in excessive quantities, often to finance budget deficits, leading to a total loss of confidence in the national currency.

The most striking historical examples are the Weimar Republic in Germany (1923), Zimbabwe in the 2000s, or Venezuela starting in 2016. In these cases, the currency lost its function as a store of value and a medium of exchange, pushing populations toward alternative currencies or barter.

The risk of hyperinflation is a central argument for bitcoiners, who highlight the supply limited to 21 million units of BTC as protection against this kind of monetary excess. Unlike fiat currencies, no authority can arbitrarily increase the quantity of bitcoins in circulation.

entries.title: TIMESTAMP
entries.body:
Timestamping, or “*timestamp*” in English, is a mechanism that consists of associating a precise time marker with an event, a piece of data or a message. In the general context of computer systems, timestamping is used to determine the chronological order of operations and to verify the integrity of data over time.

In the specific case of Bitcoin, timestamps make it possible to establish the chronology of transactions and blocks. Each block in the blockchain contains a timestamp indicating the approximate time of its creation. Satoshi Nakamoto even speaks of a “timestamp server”, in his *White Paper*, to describe what would today be called the “blockchain”. The role of timestamping on Bitcoin is to determine the chronology of transactions, in order to be able to determine, without the intervention of a central authority, which transaction arrived first. This mechanism allows each user to verify the non-existence of a transaction in the past, and thus to prevent a malicious user from carrying out a double spend. This mechanism is justified by Satoshi Nakamoto in his *White Paper* by the famous sentence: “*The only way to confirm the absence of a transaction is to be aware of all transactions.*” This standard is based on Unix time, which represents the total number of seconds elapsed since January 1, 1970.

*Block timestamps are relatively flexible on Bitcoin, because for a timestamp to be considered valid, it simply needs to be greater than the median time of the 11 blocks preceding it (MTP) and less than the median of the times returned by the nodes (network-adjusted time) plus 2 hours.*

entries.title: UNIX TIME
entries.body:
Unix Time represents the number of seconds elapsed since January 1, 1970 at midnight UTC (the Unix Epoch). This system is used in Unix operating systems and their derivatives to mark time in a universal and standardized way. It allows clock synchronization and the management of events over time, independently of time zones.

In the context of Bitcoin, it is used for the local clock of nodes, and therefore for the calculation of the NAT. The network-adjusted time is a median of the nodes' times calculated locally by each node, and this reference is then used to verify the validity of block timestamps. Indeed, for a block to be accepted by a node, its timestamp must lie between the MTP (median time of the last 11 blocks mined) and the NAT plus 2 hours:

```text
MTP < Horodatage valide < (NAT + 2h)
```

Unix Time is also used to establish *timelocks*, when these are based on real time, and not on a number of blocks.
